items.title: ASUS Store Hack — Expect Fake Order Emails
items.summary: ASUS, the company that makes laptops and computer parts, says someone got into its online store and took customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, and order records. No card numbers were taken. The danger now is fake messages that quote your real order to sound believable. If an email or a call asks you to confirm an ASUS order, don't click and don't call the number it gives you — open your browser and type asus.com yourself. I've seen these; they always rush you.

items.title: Is your computer still under factory warranty? Dell, HP and Lenovo look it up free from the serial number on the sticker
items.summary: Turn the laptop over, or look at the back of a desktop tower, and find the white sticker with the serial number. On a Dell it is called the Service Tag — seven letters and numbers. Type it into the maker's own page: dell.com/support for Dell, support.hp.com for HP, and pcsupport.lenovo.com for Lenovo (look for warranty lookup there). It shows the exact date your coverage ends, in seconds, with no account to create. Write that date on a piece of tape and stick it to the bottom of the machine. It settles arguments later.

items.title: Grandma's cassette tapes won't last forever — Audacity is the free app at audacityteam.org that records them onto your computer as MP3s
items.summary: Go to audacityteam.org and download Audacity — it is free, open source, and runs on Windows and Mac. You will need a cord from the tape deck's headphone or line-out jack into your computer's microphone or line-in jack (a few dollars at Walmart or on Amazon). Open Audacity, press Record, press Play on the tape deck, and let the whole side run through. Then use File > Export to save it as an MP3 you can email, put on a flash drive, or burn to a CD. Nothing is uploaded anywhere — the whole thing happens on your own machine, with no account and no internet needed.

items.title: Weber Shut Off Its June Oven's App — Check Whether Your Own Smart Gadgets Still Work
items.summary: Last Tuesday, Weber switched off the servers behind its June countertop oven. People paid up to $1,500, and now the app, the camera, and the guided cooking are gone — the oven only bakes. Nothing broke; the company just turned it off. Any gadget in your house that runs on the maker's servers can be next. The two-minute check: open the app for each smart device you own. If it cannot work without signing in to the company's account, that gadget has an expiration date.

items.title: Google put Gemini on your Windows PC for free — install it from gemini.google/desktop and press Alt+Space to ask it anything
items.summary: Go to gemini.google/desktop and download the free Gemini app for Windows (it runs on Windows 10 and 11). Then press Alt and Space together, and a small box opens right on top of whatever you are doing. Ask it to rewrite an email so it sounds kinder, explain a letter you got in the mail, put a long article into three sentences, or give you a recipe from what is already in your fridge. It is free with your Google account, and it stays out of the way until you call for it.

items.title: New laptops are about to cost 5% to 20% more — Windows' own Settings > System > About shows whether yours can go another year
items.summary: Click Start, type about, and open About your PC — the same page as Settings > System > About. It names your processor and shows how much working space your apps have to run in. Write those two lines down on paper. Now here is the news: Acer's chief executive said this week that computer prices will climb another 5% to 20% by the end of 2026, because the parts inside have been getting more expensive all year. So before you spend on a new machine, let somebody look at the one you own. If it is healthy inside, a good going-over and a fresh setup can keep it running for years — and if you truly do need a new one, buying sooner is cheaper than buying in December.

items.title: That Call About a Warrant Is a Scam — Real Police Never Demand Money
items.summary: If your phone rings and the caller says you missed jury duty, or that a judge signed a paper for your arrest, hang up — it's a scam. Callers fake the real number of your local sheriff's office, keep you on the line, and take payment in gift cards, wires or cash. Police never phone you to collect money. Hang up, then call the sheriff's office at a number you look up yourself.

items.title: A file called photo.jpg.exe is not a photo — turn on "File name extensions" in Windows File Explorer to see a file's real name
items.summary: Open any folder, click View at the top of the window, point to Show, and click File name extensions. Now every file shows its real ending. A file named photo.jpg is a picture; one named photo.jpg.exe is a program wearing a picture's name. Windows hides those endings by default, and that's exactly what scammers count on. It's free, it's already on every Windows PC, and it takes about ten seconds.

items.title: That Amazon "deal" price may be higher than it was last month — CamelCamelCamel shows the real price history free at camelcamelcamel.com
items.summary: Copy the web address of the Amazon item you're looking at, paste it into the search box at camelcamelcamel.com (yes, that's the real name), and you'll get a simple chart of what it actually cost over the past months — including the lowest price it has ever been. You can set a free alert, and it will email you when the price really drops. You don't need an account just to look up a price.

items.title: Microsoft's September Patches May Have Quietly Stopped Your Backups
items.summary: Microsoft says the patches it sent out this month can quietly stop the tool that copies your files for you. On some computers the last-backup date freezes, Windows keeps asking you to reconnect a perfectly good drive, and older versions of your files disappear. No scam to spot here — nothing was stolen; the safety net just stopped working. Press Start, type File History, and check that date. If it's stale, copy your Documents, Pictures and Desktop onto a USB drive until Microsoft ships a fix.

items.title: Chrome will start warning you about old-style "not private" websites in October — turn on Always Use Secure Connections now in Chrome's Settings
items.summary: Starting in October, Google Chrome will begin warning you before it opens an older-style website that doesn't have the little padlock. You can turn that protection on right now instead of waiting. Open Chrome, click the three dots at the top right, then Settings > Privacy and security > Security, and switch on Always use secure connections. It's free and takes under a minute.

items.title: That shocking photo might be AI — Chrome's built-in "About this image" check tells you in one right-click, free and built in
items.summary: If a picture in your feed looks too wild to be true, you can check it. In Chrome, right-click the photo and choose About this image. Google looks for a hidden, invisible mark called SynthID that it adds to pictures made with its AI tools, and it tells you what it finds. It's free and already built into Chrome — nothing to install.
